analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress from ever becoming lobbyists and tightens the revolving door for staff and lobbying firms.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 7 cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on May 21, 2025 and has had no hearing, committee vote, or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar any former Senator, Representative, or elected congressional officer from lobbying Congress for life. It would stretch the current one-year cooling-off period for senior congressional staff to six years, and would bar registered lobbyists and foreign agents from taking congressional jobs for six years if they lobbied the offices they would join. It would also force lobbying firms to disclose which former members and senior staffers they employ, publish that information on a searchable public website (lobbyists.gov), and raise the maximum fine for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who want lawmakers to answer to them rather than to future employers. The bill would make it far riskier and less lucrative for members of Congress and senior staff to sell their access after leaving office, and would give the public a searchable record of which lobbying firms employ former insiders. Government watchdog groups have long pushed for these kinds of cooling-off rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want insider lobbying curbed

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a lifetime lobbying ban on former Senators, Representatives, and elected congressional officers, with criminal penalties under section 216 of title 18.
Extends the post-employment restriction for congressional staff from 1 year to 6 years.

Bars registered lobbyists and agents of foreign principals from being hired by a Member or committee they lobbied for 6 years, subject to a waiver by the chamber's ethics committee for 'compelling national need'.

Requires firms with more than 3 registered lobbyists to disclose annually every former member and senior staffer they employ, reportable on a public searchable database and forwarded to the U.S. Attorney for D.C. for enforcement review.
Creates a joint, easily searchable public website, lobbyists.gov, for lobbyist disclosures, and raises the maximum civil penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000.

analysis.who_pays: The lobbying industry, law firms, and trade associations that hire former members and senior staff for their access, and members of Congress and senior staff who would lose a well-worn path to six- and seven-figure private-sector jobs. Taxpayers would fund a $100,000 appropriation for the new disclosure website.

drawbacks.text: The lifetime ban on members and six-year restrictions are far harsher than current rules, and some critics argue such broad post-employment bans can deter able people from running for or serving in Congress and can push influence-seeking into informal channels that are harder to track.

The bill includes a waiver: either chamber's ethics committee can exempt a person from the lobbyist-to-Congress hiring ban based on a 'compelling national need', leaving room for case-by-case exceptions.
The bill relies on disclosure and existing criminal penalties rather than creating a new enforcement body, so its effect depends on prosecutors actually pursuing violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but favors the public: Congress writing lifetime and six-year cooling-off rules would sharply reduce the market value of insider access, at the cost of some career freedom for ex-members and staff and some risk that influence moves into channels the rules don't cover. The disclosure database and penalty increase are cheap and add genuine public visibility. The waiver clause and reliance on existing enforcement are the main design weaknesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee in May 2025, and has sat there without a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action ever since.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse (D-CO) introduced the Close the Revolving Door Act of 2025 on May 21, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is the only action the bill has received.
The bill has 7 cosponsors, all Democrats.

The full text of the bill specifies a lifetime lobbying ban for members, a 6-year restriction for congressional staff, a 6-year hiring ban for lobbyists who lobbied the offices they would join, new disclosure requirements for large lobbying firms, a public lobbyists.gov database, and an increased maximum penalty of $500,000.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the lobbying industry and firms that profit from hiring former members and senior staff are better off, because the bill has not moved toward a vote.

for.name: Rep. Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and laid out a package of lifetime lobbying bans, staff cooling-off extensions, disclosure rules, and higher penalties.

for.name: 7 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or any committee action on the bill since it was referred on May 21, 2025.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor; the bill is not scheduled for a vote and has no Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has ever been held, so there is no roll call to score; the only visible support so far is 7 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican endorsers.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and government relations shops
industries.note: The bill bans former members from lobbying for life, extends staff cooling-off to six years, and requires firms with more than three lobbyists to disclose every former insider on their payroll. Firms currently sell the access and relationships of ex-lawmakers and ex-staff, so the bill would shrink both their hiring pipeline and the market for it.

industries.industry: Law firms and consultancies that employ former members and senior staff
industries.note: Hiring a former Senator or a former chief of staff is a revenue driver because clients pay for introductions on Capitol Hill. Mandatory public disclosure of those hires, reported to a federal prosecutor, would make that business more visible and riskier.

Agents of foreign principals would face the same six-year hiring ban for offices they lobbied, cutting off one route by which foreign influence operations have placed people inside congressional offices.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to House committees never get a hearing or a vote, and this one has shown no movement since its May 2025 referral. With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action in months, it is very unlikely to advance in this Congress unless a watchdog scandal forces the issue or it is folded into a larger ethics package.
